The teal independents are in a similar place on the political spectrum to the United Kingdom’s Liberal Democrats, who hold 72 seats in the House of Commons. In Australia’s changing scene, they have similarities to a reinvigorated Australian Democrats, founded by former Liberal minister Don Chipp.

A looming challenge for the teal independents is what to do when, inevitably, they win the balance of power. There is a high chance that the 2028 federal election will see Albanese Labor lose seats and One Nation, the Greens and teal independents gain seats. Labor may keep its majority, but at some point that balance of power outcome is inevitable. What then?

Independents without some form of cohesion are easy pickings. The first threat by Labor will be to ask the governor-general to have it seek a vote of confidence in the House of Representatives. Without others to give Labor a majority, this would effectively force the independent teals to back Labor – or Coalition/One Nation – or face another election. In the case of another election, Australia’s right-wing media would be in full-throttle condemnation of the independents and anyone else on the crossbench for not supporting a new government.

More likely, the independents would be picked off by inducements from Labor or the conservative blocs. Offers might include the speakership or ministries, or hospitals, school halls, convention centres, sports grounds and better roads in home electorates. Perhaps there would be an underwhelming promise of a “reduction” – not a total ending – of approvals for new or expanded coalmines, gas fracking or forest logging. Without cohesion, the teal independents may end up losers, not the powerhouse they could be.

There is rumour and speculation about whether they will form a party. Don’t expect the press gallery in Canberra to think much outside the conventional bubble of two-party politics. It will tend to vilify rather than simply cover such a transformation to consolidate the teal independents’ power.

A teals party could allow freedom of conscience for its members on all matters. It would not be burdened by the forced solidarity of a party such as Labor. Similar freedom was allowed within the Democrats, and the Australian Greens’ party constitution allows for freedom of conscience for its representatives, except those from New South Wales, which required an exclusion clause when the constitution was adopted.

A teals party, under a suitable new name, would set out its basic objectives, including more action to tackle climate change. Party status would avoid the restrictive clauses for independents in the recent Labor–Coalition legislation giving parties privileged fundraising and election spending options.

The teal independents will need to be united in intent. The opportunity to form a government, ready to confront corporate intransigence in the face of global inequity and breakdown, should not be lost. Simple as that.

There are, however, other good alternatives to becoming a traditional party.

One fine option would be for the teal independents to agree to a set of guidelines for negotiating as a group, to use the best possible leverage when minority government comes. For example, they could adopt baseline requirements for tackling the climate emergency or corruption. They could have an established mandate for post-election negotiations.

This would not be new. Five independents, called “The Independents”, including myself, were elected to the balance of power in the Tasmanian House of Assembly in 1989. We had a set of agreed requirements to put to Labor and the Liberals in order for them to form government. We negotiated with both parties and, when the Liberals dropped out, signed a Labor–Green accord that achieved many of the requirements we had set out, including prohibiting the proposed Wesley Vale pulp mill, enlarging the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area, the introduction of freedom of information legislation and an end to public funding for ministerial liquor cabinets.

After the accord was signed, the independents and our supporters set up the Tasmanian Greens and helped, in 1992, to formulate the Australian Greens. At the next election Labor lost office but all five independents were re-elected as Greens. That’s a direction in which the teal independents are not likely to go.

A third alternative would be for the teal independents to simply agree to negotiate en bloc in any future post-election scenario. This minimalist position would obviate the risk of them being played off against each other or picked off one by one. They would be committed to working together and equally negotiating an outcome.

In democracies in recent centuries, parties began forming to pursue the special interests of various sections of society, especially financial self-interests. More recently still, green parties arose around the world, as if by spontaneous combustion, to tackle the looming ecological crises, including climate change, forest destruction and species extinctions. That inevitably led them to also promote social justice, peace and democracy.

Money rules, however. Democracies – just like autocracies – are overridden by the corporate rich who wield the financial power of advertising, media ownership, lobbying and political donations. You only have to look as far as the recent gift of a plane from Gina Rinehart to Pauline Hanson, or see the weapons manufacturers’ billboards around Canberra Airport, or count up the 800 lobbyists who work in our capital.

Two factors are leading to a national and global showdown in human affairs: the environmental crisis, including global heating threatening prosperity, and the growing gap between rich and poor, which is a potent flux for civil disruption.

In Australia – one of the richest per capita countries on Earth if its resource base is considered – these factors are stalking politics and are destroying the time-honoured two-party political system. They shaped the emergence of the Greens and the teal independents and the fierce big-end-of-town opposition to both, although a portion of those rich voters, alarmed by the global crises, is shearing off.

Recent elections have shown voter support for the old parties dropping consistently. The 2028 election will likely see the lowest vote for the Coalition and Labor in history. Labor, duchessed by corporate interests, has replaced the Coalition as Australia’s right of centre party, leaving the Coalition splintering even further right, to territory it’s now unsuccessfully fighting over with One Nation.

The teal independents have occupied the middle ground abandoned by both the Liberals and Labor. The Greens have taken over much of the Labor left’s traditional concern for the environment; the least well-off citizens; human rights, including First Nations’ rights; and opposition to overseas military involvement.

The above analysis is contestable but gives an insight into what is not contestable – the collapse of the once-entrenched two-party system.

Here’s the crunch question emerging from that collapse: given that a new polyglot right could form a future government, can a new polyglot left? That is, if or when the teals and Greens win more seats than Labor, how do the teal independents take due control of their situation? A question that precedes that question is whether the teal independents and Greens should swap preferences before directing votes to Labor or the Coalition.

The appearance of teal independents as a grouping is already there. Their coherence should not be missing when the crunch comes. Some form of publicly understood agreement needs to be embraced.

The global economy could face a 50 per cent loss in GDP between 2070 and 2090 unless immediate policy action is taken on risks posed by the climate crisis, warns a new report by the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries in the UK. Billions of people will die in this scenario.

As the Albanese government fails to measure up, and the Coalition and One Nation offer denial and inaction, here’s a possible outcome of an election down the line as the climate crisis worsens:

The House of Representatives has 150 seats, so a majority is 76. In the climate crisis with the economy collapsing, Labor wins 40. The Coalition/One Nation/right independents win 34. The Greens and teal independents each win 38, totalling 76.

It will require the independents as well as the Greens being prepared to act together to form a crisis-management government. Assuming the age-old enmity between Labor and the Coalition and other right parties, the teal independents will need to be united in intent. The opportunity to form a government, ready to confront corporate intransigence in the face of global inequity and breakdown, should not be lost. Simple as that.

Regardless of prognostications about Australia’s political future, it is healthy to talk about the alternatives that may be coming for voters. The teals will, of course, choose for themselves between remaining isolated independents or achieving some form of togetherness in the face of the unprecedented forces and fortunes challenging national politics.

It is a classic case of doing nothing being a decision of very great consequence.

Bob Brown is a former leader of the Australian Greens. His latest book is Defiance: Stories from Nature and Its Defenders.
